justification: Abstract's object is consensus formation via iterative inter-agent message exchange, and the contribution is a world-model+RL attacker acting on that interaction; preliminary results are lab runs against a prompt baseline.

Contribution is a credibility score learned from past contributions and used to aggregate team outputs, i.e. the arrangement of who counts; lab experiments across tasks and adversary-majority settings, no deployment.

Credited mechanism is bandit-based adaptive sampling that spends more agent calls on harder inputs; evaluated in the lab on two labelled datasets (AEGIS 2.0, SWMH), not in a deployed screening service.

Contribution is a multi-agent architecture whose ToM, BDI beliefs and symbolic solver govern collaborative decision-making; the study varies those components across LLMs on a lab resource-allocation task.
REDEREF's claim is belief-guided delegation and re-routing of work among agents; evidence is lab runs on split-knowledge tasks compared with random recursive delegation, no real deployment.

Contribution is a diagnostic theory plus SFS metric characterising why closed-system multi-step and debate loops degrade faithfulness, generalising past one mechanism; evidence is 16 lab conditions on SciFact and FEVER.
MAS-FIRE is an instrument: a 15-type fault taxonomy and injection harness for measuring MAS reliability, not a loop mechanism; faults are injected into three research MAS architectures in the lab.

The mechanism studied is verifier/corrector dosing and delay that decides whether false claims are suppressed; a closed-form threshold is derived and then confirmed by lab runs across five open models.

A position piece arguing for active dynamic moderation and governance deciding whether MAS output may stand, with no study or data reported; the paper is explicitly labelled Position and offers argument only.
Object is task assignment and coordination across agents, comparing orchestrator versus planner allocation; evidence is lab experiments varying worker-capability information, no field setting.
MasRouter decides collaboration mode, role allocation and per-agent LLM choice, i.e. the arrangement itself; validated in the lab on MBPP and HumanEval against SOTA routing baselines.

The contribution is a confidence-normalised pooling rule and a study of how topology (centralised vs distributed) governs collective judgement; a systematic lab study on a misinformation-detection task.
Studies how the number of interacting agents shapes collective dynamics, plus a mean-field model of that population effect; evidence is simulated coordination games in the lab, no real deployment.
Object is peer influence between agents and how peer information is presented, and how herd tendency can be tuned to improve collaboration; a series of controlled lab experiments, not a field study.
LEGOMem's contribution is procedural memory units, where they are placed and how they are retrieved across orchestrators and agents; evaluated in the lab on the OfficeBench benchmark.

The mechanism is an agent-driven audit that judges prompt-specification consistency, run under a locked protocol; it is applied to AEGIS, a real seven-lane production pipeline, and studies what happened over nine rounds.

ALLURE's mechanism is an outer loop that rewrites the evaluator's in-context examples from its own deviations, improving the judge between rounds; the abstract proposes and argues for the approach with no results reported.

ARCF's core is a Reliability Control Layer that monitors execution, detects MAST failure types and triggers verified recovery, i.e. a runtime check; evidence is simulation over enterprise workflows, not a production study.
The reported finding is about the architect/coder role split in a two-agent workflow and which role is the bottleneck; it documents what the authors observed in one of their own development projects.

Same quantum_bench workflow: the claim is that the architect role, not the coder role, is the reliability bottleneck, evidenced by 21 errors documented across five groups in the authors' own single project.

RedDebate's mechanism is agents critiquing one another's reasoning so unsafe responses are revised, with memory carrying insights forward; validated in the lab on safety benchmarks across several models.

LLM-proposed diagnostic plans are checked and ranked by an external causal-inference model and an Evaluator Agent before being recommended; results compare augmented against unaugmented plans in a prototype, not a deployment.

The variable studied is architecture, fixed workflow versus single-agent versus multi-agent versus general code agents, and its iteration depth; a controlled lab comparison on a unified patching benchmark.

The mechanism is a critic agent that challenges the primary agent's conclusions before release to human reviewers, a pre-submission gate; evidence is a with/without comparison over 500 expert-validated cases.

Contribution is a calculus of when locally passing evaluator checks fail to compose, for systems whose outputs need external evaluator authorisation; the paper explicitly disclaims benchmark-complete validation.
